html:
The big picture

The lecture finishes rotational dynamics and then turns from rigid bodies to bodies that can tip over or stretch. (1) A ball rolling without slipping both moves and spins, v = \omega r, so its energy is E_\text{kin,trans} + E_\text{kin,rot} + E_\text{pot}; part of the height goes into spinning, so it reaches the bottom of a ramp slower than a sliding block, v = \sqrt{\tfrac{10}{7}gH} against \sqrt{2gH}. Forces and torques give the same result, a = \tfrac57 g\sin\theta, and the friction force that makes it roll. (2) Conservation of angular momentum without external torque: a person running on a free platform turns the platform the other way. (3) A torque perpendicular to \vec L turns \vec L instead of growing it: a spinning wheel held at one end precesses at \omega_p = \frac{m r g}{J\omega_d}. (4) Seen from a rotating frame, an object moving in it is pushed sideways by the Coriolis force, \vec a_{c,\text{app}} = 2\vec v\times\vec\omega; on Earth it depends on the latitude. (5) A body in equilibrium can be stable, unstable or neutral; it stays upright while the vertical line through its centre of gravity stays inside its base. (6) Real solids deform: a tensile test gives stress \sigma = F/A_0 against strain \varepsilon = \Delta L/L_0; in the linear elastic range \sigma = E\varepsilon with Young's modulus E; beyond the yield strength the deformation is plastic (permanent), and the peak of the curve is the ultimate tensile strength.

1 Rolling: rotation plus translation

Lecture: p. 3 bottom – p. 4 · Giancoli §10-9

So far a body either moved (translation, 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 7 Kinetic energy and the work–energy principle) or spun about a fixed axis (13 Collisions, Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum › 7 Moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy). A ball rolling down a ramp does both at once. The lecture asks: what is the velocity of the ball leaving the ramp? It starts at rest, v_0 = 0, \omega_0 = 0.

Rolling without slipping. If the ball doesn't slide, the point touching the ramp is at rest for that instant, and the centre moves forward exactly one circumference per turn. So the speed of the centre and the angular velocity are linked, as on the board ("rolling ball"):

\omega_{e,r} = \frac{v_{e,r}}{r}
Symbols
  • v_{e,r} — speed of the ball's centre at the end of the ramp ("e" end, "r" rolling) (m/s)
  • \omega_{e,r} — angular velocity of the ball about its centre at the end (rad/s)
  • r — the ball's radius (m); the figure writes r_0
Intuition — why v = \omega r only when rolling

Sit on the ball's centre and watch: the ground slides backwards under you at v, and the rim turns at \omega r. If these two speeds match, the rim's bottom point moves with the ground: no sliding. If v \neq \omega r, the ball skids (a car spinning its wheels, or a bowling ball that slides before it starts to roll), and the relation doesn't hold.

Energy. Rolling without slipping wastes no energy: the friction at the contact point is static friction, and it acts at a point that is not moving, so it does no work (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 5 Work done by a constant force). Mechanical energy is conserved, but now the kinetic energy has two parts (board: "conservation of energy"):

\frac12 m\cdot v_0^2 + \frac12 J\cdot\omega_0^2 + m\cdot g\cdot H_0 = \frac12 m\cdot v_e^2 + \frac12 J\cdot\omega_e^2 + m\cdot g\cdot H_1
Symbols
  • \tfrac12 m v^2 — E_\text{kin,trans}, translational kinetic energy of the centre of mass (J); m — mass of the ball (kg)
  • \tfrac12 J\omega^2 — E_\text{kin,rot}, rotational kinetic energy about the centre (J); J — moment of inertia about an axis through the centre (kg·m²)
  • m g H — E_\text{pot}, potential energy (J); H_0, H_1 — height of the centre at start and end (m), H_0 - H_1 = H
  • subscripts 0 — at the start, e — at the end of the ramp; g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}

Insert the start values (v_0 = 0, \omega_0 = 0), measure heights from the end (H_1 = 0, H_0 = H), take J = \tfrac25 m r^2 for a solid sphere (13 Collisions, Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum › 7 Moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy, table row (e)) and \omega_e = v_e/r:

\begin{aligned} 0 + 0 + m g H &= \tfrac12 m v_e^2 + \tfrac12\cdot\underbrace{\tfrac25 m r^2}_{J}\cdot\frac{v_e^2}{r^2} && \text{(insert } J \text{ and } \omega_e = v_e/r) \\ g H &= \tfrac12 v_e^2 + \tfrac15 v_e^2 && \text{(divide by } m;\ r^2 \text{ cancels)} \\ g H &= \left(\tfrac5{10} + \tfrac2{10}\right) v_e^2 = \tfrac7{10}\, v_e^2 && \text{(common denominator 10)} \\ v_{e,r} &= \sqrt{\tfrac{10}7\cdot g\cdot H} && \text{(multiply by } \tfrac{10}7\text{, take the positive root)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Neither the mass nor the radius is left: every solid sphere, marble or bowling ball, arrives with the same speed. Compare to free fall (or sliding with \mu_d = 0), where all of mgH becomes translational energy (12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions):

v_{e,f} = \sqrt{2\cdot g\cdot H} \ >\ v_{e,r} \qquad \text{as} \quad 2 > \frac{10}7
Symbols
  • v_{e,f} — end speed of a body falling (or sliding without friction) through the height H (m/s); "f" free fall
  • v_{e,r} — end speed of the rolling sphere (m/s), from above

The rolling ball is slower, not because friction brakes it (it does no work), but because \tfrac27 of the energy goes into spinning: \tfrac12 J\omega^2 = \tfrac15 m v^2 against \tfrac12 m v^2.

Common mistake — "the heavier (or bigger) ball rolls down faster"

Mass and radius cancel completely: v = \sqrt{\frac{2gH}{1 + J/(m r^2)}} depends only on H and the shape factor J/(m r^2) (\tfrac25 sphere, \tfrac12 solid cylinder, 1 hoop). A marble and a bowling ball tie; a hoop loses to both, whatever its mass.

Forces acting on the sphere. The same problem with Newton's laws gives the acceleration and the friction force, which energy cannot give.

Translation of the centre of mass along x (down the slope positive):

m\cdot g\cdot\sin\theta - F_R = m\cdot a
Symbols
  • m — mass of the sphere (kg) (the figure writes M); \theta — angle of the ramp
  • m g\sin\theta — component of the weight along the slope (N), driving the ball down (9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction)
  • F_R — static friction force at the contact point (N), up the slope
  • a — acceleration of the centre of mass along x (m/s²)

Rotation about the centre: of all forces only F_R has a lever arm (F_N and the weight point through the centre). Its torque turns the ball faster (rotational F = ma, 13 Collisions, Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum › 10 Angular momentum):

\sum T = J\cdot\dot\omega = r_0\cdot F_R = \frac25 m\, r_0^2\cdot\dot\omega, \qquad \omega = \frac{v}{r_0}\ \Rightarrow\ \dot\omega = \frac{\dot v}{r_0} = \frac{a}{r_0}
Symbols
  • \sum T — net torque about the sphere's centre (N·m); J = \tfrac25 m r_0^2 — the sphere's moment of inertia (kg·m²)
  • \dot\omega = \mathrm d\omega/\mathrm dt — angular acceleration (rad/s²); r_0 — radius (m), the lever arm of F_R
  • \omega = v/r_0 — the rolling condition; differentiated in time, it links \dot\omega and a = \dot v

Now solve the two equations together:

\begin{aligned} r_0 F_R &= \tfrac25 m r_0^2\cdot\frac{a}{r_0} && (\dot\omega = a/r_0) \\ F_R &= \tfrac25\, m\cdot a && \text{(divide by } r_0;\ r_0 \text{ cancels)} \\ m g\sin\theta - \tfrac25 m a &= m a && \text{(insert } F_R \text{ into the } x \text{ equation)} \\ g\sin\theta &= \tfrac75\, a && \text{(divide by } m,\ \text{add } \tfrac25 a) \\ a &= \tfrac57\cdot g\cdot\sin\theta && (\times\tfrac57) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Less than g\sin\theta for a sliding block: the friction force is needed to spin the ball up, so it takes away from the push along the slope. The result agrees with the energy route: the ramp is s = H/\sin\theta long, and v^2 = 2as = 2\cdot\tfrac57 g\sin\theta\cdot\frac{H}{\sin\theta} = \tfrac{10}7 gH ✓.

Why may friction appear in the force equation but not in the energy equation?

In the force equation friction is a real force on the ball: without it the ball would slide and not spin (on ice it slides down at g\sin\theta without turning). In the energy equation only work counts, W = \int\vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s at the point where the force acts. Friction acts at the contact point, which is momentarily at rest, so \mathrm d\vec s = \vec 0 there and W = 0. Friction moves energy from translation into rotation without destroying any. Only if the ball slips does friction act at a moving point and turn energy into heat.

Intuition — how much friction is needed?

With a = \tfrac57 g\sin\theta: F_R = \tfrac25 m a = \tfrac27 m g\sin\theta. Static friction can give at most \mu_s F_N = \mu_s m g\cos\theta, so the ball rolls without slipping only while \tfrac27\tan\theta \le \mu_s. On a steep or icy ramp it rolls and slips, and the formulas above no longer hold.

Worked example — a solid cylinder on a 30° ramp

A solid cylinder (J = \tfrac12 m r^2) rolls from rest down a ramp of height H = 1.2\ \mathrm m at \theta = 30°.

  1. Energy: m g H = \tfrac12 m v^2 + \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 m r^2\cdot\frac{v^2}{r^2} = \tfrac34 m v^2, so v = \sqrt{\tfrac43 gH} = \sqrt{\tfrac43\cdot9.81\cdot1.2} = 3.96\ \mathrm{m/s} (sphere: 4.10\ \mathrm{m/s}, sliding: 4.85\ \mathrm{m/s}).
  2. Forces: torque r F_R = \tfrac12 m r^2\cdot\frac ar gives F_R = \tfrac12 m a; then m g\sin\theta - \tfrac12 m a = m a, so a = \tfrac23 g\sin\theta = 3.27\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.
  3. Check: s = H/\sin\theta = 2.4\ \mathrm m, v = \sqrt{2as} = \sqrt{2\cdot3.27\cdot2.4} = 3.96\ \mathrm{m/s} ✓.
  4. Friction needed: F_R = \tfrac13 m g\sin\theta, so it rolls if \mu_s \ge \tfrac13\tan30° = 0.19.
Problem-solving steps — rolling without slipping
  1. Draw the forces: weight at the centre, normal force and static friction at the contact point; pick x along the slope.
  2. Fast route for speeds: energy with both kinetic terms, m g H = \tfrac12 m v^2 + \tfrac12 J\omega^2, and \omega = v/r.
  3. For acceleration or friction: \sum F_x = m a for the centre, \sum T = J\dot\omega about the centre, linked by \dot\omega = a/r.
  4. Solve; check F_R \le \mu_s F_N (otherwise the body slips) and that mass and radius dropped out.

2 Why does a rolling ball slow down? Rolling friction

Lecture: p. 4 bottom – p. 5 top ("rolling friction?") · Giancoli §10-10

The board ends with a question, "rolling friction?", and a sketch: a ball rolling to the right with \vec v on flat ground, a force \vec F at its bottom pointing to the left, and next to it \sum_i\vec F_i = m\cdot\vec a.

Filling the gaps — the paradox behind the question

A ball rolling on a level floor does slow down eventually, so by \sum\vec F = m\vec a some force must point backwards: the \vec F at the contact point in the sketch. But the torque of that same backward force about the centre turns the ball faster in its rolling direction. So the force slows the translation but speeds up the rotation, and the rolling condition v = \omega r can't hold for both. The way out: real bodies are not rigid. Ball and floor flatten slightly, the contact is a small patch, and the floor pushes up harder on the front half of the patch than on the back. The normal force F_N then acts a small distance \ell in front of the centre and has a torque F_N\,\ell that slows the rotation. That is rolling friction, F_F = \mu_W F_N in 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction › 5 Rolling friction and rope friction.

3 Conservation of angular momentum: person on a platform

Lecture: p. 1 top – middle · Giancoli §11-1, §11-6

This continues 13 Collisions, Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum › 11 Conservation of angular momentum: without external torque, the total angular momentum of a system stays constant. Example.

Given: m_p = 60\ \mathrm{kg}, r = 6\ \mathrm m, J_{pf} = 1800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}, v = 4.2\ \mathrm{m/s}. Person and platform start at rest, so the total angular momentum is zero and stays zero (the bearing is frictionless: no external torque about the axis; the push of the feet on the platform is internal):

L_p + L_{pf} = 0, \qquad J_p\,\omega_p\cdot\vec e_z + J_{pf}\cdot\vec\omega_{pf} = 0
Symbols
  • L_p, L_{pf} — angular momentum of person and platform about the axis (kg·m²/s)
  • J_p = m_p r^2 — the person's moment of inertia, treated as a point mass at distance r (kg·m²); \omega_p = v_p/r — the person's angular velocity (rad/s)
  • J_{pf} — the platform's moment of inertia (kg·m²); \vec\omega_{pf} — its angular velocity vector (rad/s)
  • \vec e_z — unit vector along the axis, upward: the person runs counter-clockwise seen from above
  • v_p = 4.2\ \mathrm{m/s} — the person's speed relative to the ground (not to the platform)

Insert J_p = m_p r^2 and \omega_p = v_p/r (one r cancels, ticked in green on the board) and solve for the platform:

m_p\, r^2\cdot\frac{v_p}{r}\cdot\vec e_z + J_{pf}\cdot\vec\omega_{pf} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \vec\omega_{pf} = -\,m_p\, r\, v_p\cdot\frac{1}{J_{pf}}\,\vec e_z

Symbols as above. The minus sign: the platform turns opposite to the person.

Unclear (p. 1): the radius and the result

The board writes r = 6\ \mathrm m and a result that reads like "\approx 1.4\ \mathrm{m/s}" (hard to read; the unit should be rad/s). In the textbook example the board copies, 6.0 m is the platform's diameter, so r = 3.0\ \mathrm m and \omega_{pf} = \frac{60\cdot3.0\cdot4.2}{1800}\ \mathrm{rad/s} = 0.42\ \mathrm{rad/s} (one turn in about 15 s). With r = 6\ \mathrm m as written, \omega_{pf} = \frac{60\cdot6\cdot4.2}{1800}\ \mathrm{rad/s} = 0.84\ \mathrm{rad/s}. Neither gives 1.4. Units check: \frac{\mathrm{kg\cdot m\cdot m/s}}{\mathrm{kg\,m^2}} = \mathrm{1/s} = \mathrm{rad/s} ✓.

The board then sets the two laws side by side:

\text{change of linear momentum:}\ \ \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = \sum\vec F_i, \qquad \text{change of angular momentum:}\ \ \frac{\mathrm d\vec L}{\mathrm dt} = \sum\vec M_i = \sum_i\vec T_i
Symbols
  • \vec p — linear momentum (kg·m/s); \vec F_i — the external forces (N)
  • \vec L — angular momentum (kg·m²/s); \vec M_i = \vec T_i — the external torques (N·m). M is the German letter for torque (Drehmoment); the lecture otherwise writes T

So: no net external force ⇒ \vec p constant; no net external torque ⇒ \vec L constant.

Moving mass outwards raises J. Board sketch (red): a mass m at distance r_0 from the axis O is split into two halves \tfrac m2; one moves inward by \Delta r (to r_{1s}, the shorter red arrow), the other outward by \Delta r (to r_{1l}, the longer one); next to it J_1 < J_2.

Filling the gaps — why J_1 < J_2

Before: J_1 = m r_0^2. After:

J_2 = \frac m2\left(r_0 - \Delta r\right)^2 + \frac m2\left(r_0 + \Delta r\right)^2 = \frac m2\left(2r_0^2 + 2\Delta r^2\right) = m r_0^2 + m\,\Delta r^2 > J_1

(\Delta r: how far each half moves, m; the cross terms \mp 2r_0\Delta r cancel.) The centre of mass of the two halves is still at r_0, but because distances enter squared, the outer half gains more than the inner half loses. With \vec L conserved, \omega must then drop: the skater with arms out of note 13.

4 Precession of a spinning wheel

Lecture: p. 1 bottom – p. 2 middle ("Precession Motion", "From the top") · Giancoli §11-7

Note 13 ended with the demonstration; now the lecture computes the precession rate.

The idea. Gravity's torque about the support is \vec T = \vec r\times m\vec g: horizontal and perpendicular to the axle. By \mathrm d\vec L = \vec T\,\mathrm dt the change of \vec L is horizontal and sideways, so the tip of \vec L (and with it the axle) swings around horizontally instead of dropping. Board sketches "from the top": the support point, \vec r to the wheel, \vec L along it and \vec T perpendicular; \mathrm d\vec L \approx \vec T\cdot\mathrm dt added at the tip of \vec L; then \vec L and the new \vec L' with the small angle \Delta\varphi between them.

\Delta\vec L \approx \vec T\cdot\Delta t, \qquad T = r\cdot m\cdot g
Symbols
  • \Delta\vec L — change of the angular momentum during the short time \Delta t (kg·m²/s); \approx because \vec T turns with \vec L, exact for \Delta t \to 0
  • T — size of gravity's torque about the support (N·m); \vec r \perp m\vec g, so T = r m g
  • r — distance from the support to the wheel's centre of mass (m); m — mass of the wheel (kg)

Since \Delta\vec L \perp \vec L, the length of \vec L doesn't change, only its direction, by the small angle \Delta\varphi (arc ≈ chord):

\begin{aligned} \Delta\varphi &= \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \frac{T\cdot\Delta t}{L} && \text{(angle = arc / radius, arc} = \Delta L) \\ \omega_p &= \frac{\Delta\varphi}{\Delta t} = \frac{T\cdot\Delta t}{L\cdot\Delta t} = \frac{m\cdot r\cdot g}{L} && \text{(angular velocity of the axle; } \Delta t \text{ cancels, } T = r m g) \\ \omega_p &= \frac{m\cdot r\cdot g}{J\cdot\omega_d} && (L = J\,\omega_d) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • \Delta\varphi — angle by which the axle turns about the vertical during \Delta t (rad)
  • \omega_p — precession angular velocity: how fast the axle swings around the support (rad/s)
  • L = J\omega_d — the wheel's spin angular momentum (kg·m²/s); J — its moment of inertia about the axle (kg·m²); \omega_d — its spin rate (rad/s)
  • m, r, g — as above

The faster the wheel spins, the slower it precesses; a wheel that doesn't spin (L = 0) has nothing to turn and simply falls.

Intuition — the same as circular motion

In uniform circular motion a force perpendicular to \vec v turns \vec v without changing its length (7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion › 4 Uniform circular motion). Here a torque perpendicular to \vec L turns \vec L without changing its length. The rule "torque makes the wheel fall" only holds when \vec L is zero or parallel to \vec T.

Worked example — how fast does a bicycle wheel precess?

A wheel, m = 2.0\ \mathrm{kg}, treated as a uniform disc of radius 0.20\ \mathrm m, spins at \omega_d = 40\ \mathrm{rad/s}; its centre is r = 0.15\ \mathrm m from the support.

  1. Moment of inertia: J = \tfrac12 m R^2 = \tfrac12\cdot2.0\cdot0.20^2 = 0.040\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} (R: wheel radius).
  2. Spin angular momentum: L = J\omega_d = 0.040\cdot40 = 1.6\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}.
  3. Precession: \omega_p = \frac{m r g}{L} = \frac{2.0\cdot0.15\cdot9.81}{1.6} = 1.84\ \mathrm{rad/s}, one turn in 2\pi/1.84 = 3.4\ \mathrm s.
  4. Check the assumption: \omega_p \ll \omega_d (1.8 vs 40 rad/s), so ignoring the angular momentum of the slow precession itself was fine.

5 The Coriolis force

Lecture: p. 2 bottom – p. 3 middle · Giancoli §11-8, §11-9

Newton's laws hold in an inertial frame. On a rotating platform (or on the rotating Earth) a ball that no force acts on still seems to curve; to keep using \sum\vec F = m\vec a there, one adds inertial (fictitious) forces, like the d'Alembert force of 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction. Two appear in a rotating frame: the centrifugal force (outwards) and, for an object moving in the rotating frame, the Coriolis force, sideways.

Filling the gaps — where the 2\omega v comes from (Giancoli's route)

In the inertial frame: the ball covers the radial distance r_B - r_A = v t. Sideways it keeps A's speed \omega r_A, while B moves at \omega r_B. So after the time t it lags behind B by

s = \left(\omega r_B - \omega r_A\right) t = \omega\left(r_B - r_A\right) t = \omega\, v\, t^2

(\omega: angular velocity of the disc, rad/s; v: the ball's speed relative to the disc, m/s; t: flight time, s; r_A, r_B: distances of A and B from the axis, m). A sideways drift growing like t^2 is what a constant acceleration gives from rest, s = \tfrac12 a t^2. Comparing, \tfrac12 a_c t^2 = \omega v t^2, so a_c = 2\omega v.

The board's result:

a_c = 2\,\omega\, v
Symbols
  • a_c — Coriolis acceleration (m/s²), sideways, perpendicular to v
  • v — "velocity of the object moving away from the centre of rotation" (board), measured in the rotating frame (m/s)
  • \omega — "angular velocity of the rotating object" (board), i.e. of the rotating frame (rad/s)

As vectors (p. 3):

\vec a_{c,\text{app}} = 2\,\vec v\times\vec\omega, \qquad \vec a_c = -\vec a_{c,\text{app}} = 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v, \qquad \vec F_c = m_0\cdot\vec a_c = 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v
Symbols
  • \vec a_{c,\text{app}} — the apparent Coriolis acceleration an observer in the rotating frame sees the object take, with no real force behind it (m/s²)
  • \vec a_c — the opposite vector (m/s²): the acceleration a real force must supply to keep the object on a straight line in the rotating frame
  • \vec F_c — Coriolis force (N); m_0 — mass of the object (kg)
  • \vec\omega — angular velocity of the frame, along its axis by the right-hand rule (rad/s); \vec v — velocity relative to the frame (m/s); \times — cross product (2 Vectors and Vector Products)
  • size: \lvert\vec a_c\rvert = 2\omega v_\perp, with v_\perp the part of \vec v perpendicular to the axis
Unclear (p. 3): the mass and the sign in \vec F_c

The board writes \vec F_c = m_0\cdot\vec a_c = 2\vec\omega\times\vec v; the mass has dropped out of the last expression: it must be \vec F_c = 2\,m_0\,\vec\omega\times\vec v. Likewise "F_c = 2\cdot\omega\, v_s\sin\alpha" below needs a factor m to be a force (as written it is an acceleration). On the sign: the fictitious force felt in the rotating frame is m_0\vec a_{c,\text{app}} = -2m_0\,\vec\omega\times\vec v (Giancoli's form); the board's \vec F_c = m_0\vec a_c is the opposite vector, the real force (from a rail, a road, a gun barrel) needed to keep the object from being deflected. Both have the size 2 m_0\omega v_\perp.

Board sketches: a disc seen from above, turning counter-clockwise, with a point moving at \vec v (up) and \vec a_{c,\text{app}} (to the right) drawn at it; next to it the Earth seen from the side, rotating about its vertical axis, with a point on its surface and two small arrows.

Filling the gaps — direction check on the disc sketch

Take \vec\omega = \omega\,\vec e_z (out of the page, counter-clockwise) and \vec v = v\,\vec e_y (up the page). Then \vec a_{c,\text{app}} = 2\vec v\times\vec\omega = 2 v\omega\,(\vec e_y\times\vec e_z) = 2v\omega\,\vec e_x: to the right, as drawn. On a counter-clockwise disc (the northern hemisphere seen from above the North Pole) a moving object is deflected to the right of its motion.

On the Earth. Board sketch: the Earth with \vec\omega_e along its axis; at the equator a velocity \vec v_1 pointing north, at 45° latitude \vec v_2 pointing north along the surface, in the southern hemisphere \vec v_3. For motion along the surface towards north or south at speed v_s = 10\ \mathrm{m/s}:

v_c = v_s\cdot\sin\alpha, \qquad F_c = 2\cdot\omega\cdot v_s\cdot\sin\alpha
Symbols
  • v_s — speed along the surface, north or south (m/s); "s" surface
  • \alpha — latitude (45° in the sketch); \omega = \omega_e — the Earth's angular velocity, 2\pi per sidereal day = 7.29\cdot10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad/s}
  • v_c = v_s\sin\alpha — the part of the velocity perpendicular to the Earth's axis (m/s): only this part counts in \vec\omega\times\vec v
  • F_c — as written, the Coriolis acceleration (m/s²); times the mass it is the force (see the flag above)
Filling the gaps — why \sin\alpha

A velocity pointing north along the surface at latitude \alpha makes the angle \alpha with the Earth's axis (at the equator it is parallel to the axis, at the pole perpendicular to it). The cross product only takes the perpendicular part, v_s\sin\alpha. So: no horizontal Coriolis deflection for north–south motion at the equator (\vec v_1 \parallel \vec\omega_e), the largest at the poles. For v_s = 10\ \mathrm{m/s} at 45°: a = 2\cdot7.29\cdot10^{-5}\cdot10\cdot\sin45° = 1.03\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, about 10^{-4}\,g: invisible in a ball game, decisive for winds and long-range artillery.

Common mistake — Coriolis is the centrifugal force

The centrifugal force acts on every object in the rotating frame, even one at rest, and points outward, m\omega^2 r. The Coriolis force acts only on objects moving relative to the frame and points sideways, perpendicular to \vec v, 2m\omega v_\perp. A ball lying still on a merry-go-round feels only the first; a ball rolled across it feels both.

Worked example — Coriolis force on a car

A car, m = 1500\ \mathrm{kg}, drives north at 30\ \mathrm{m/s} (108 km/h) at latitude 46.6° (Klagenfurt).

  1. Perpendicular velocity: v_s\sin\alpha = 30\cdot\sin46.6° = 21.8\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Acceleration: a_c = 2\cdot7.29\cdot10^{-5}\cdot21.8 = 3.18\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.
  3. Force: F_c = m a_c = 1500\cdot3.18\cdot10^{-3} = 4.8\ \mathrm N, to the right of the motion (east), about 3\cdot10^{-4} of the car's weight: the tyres take it without anyone noticing.

6 Stability and balance

Lecture: p. 5 bottom – p. 6 top ("STABILITY", 20 Nov) · Giancoli §12-4

A body in equilibrium has \sum\vec F = \vec 0 and \sum T = 0 (10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 5 Torque and equilibrium: the forklift). Stability asks what happens after a small push. Three cases:

  • stable equilibrium: the body returns to its position;
  • unstable equilibrium: it moves further away;
  • neutral equilibrium: it stays in the new position (a ball on a flat table).

The pendulum shows a rule: the ball's centre of gravity hangs below the support, and every displacement lifts it by \Delta h, so gravity pulls it back. The pencil's centre of gravity is above its point of support; every tilt lowers it and creates a torque F_G\cdot x that tips it further.

Intuition — stability as a valley in the energy

Stable means: every small displacement raises the centre of gravity, E_\text{pot} = m g h goes up, and the body rolls back down into its "valley" (the board's \Delta h at the pendulum). Unstable: every displacement lowers h (the top of a hill). Neutral: h doesn't change (a flat plain). Equilibrium itself only says the ground is flat at that spot; stability says which way it curves.

Filling the gaps — why S below M is stable

On a round bottom, the contact point is always directly below M (the normal force points through the circle's centre M). Tilt the toy: M stays at the same height above the floor, but S, below M, moves sideways behind the new contact point and rises. Its weight then turns the toy back. If S were above M, a tilt would move S beyond the contact point and lower it: the toy would fall over.

Tipping a cabinet.

Rule (book and board): a body standing on a base is stable as long as the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls within its base of support. The normal force can only act inside the contact area; once the weight's line of action is outside, nothing can balance its torque. The critical position is reached when S is exactly above the edge.

Board sketches below the figure: a tall box standing upright — "global stable"; a flat box lying on its long side — "global stable", with F_R = \mu\cdot F_N written under it; a box balanced on one corner with F_G exactly above the contact point and F_N below it — "locally stable".

Filling the gaps — reading the three boxes

The flat box is "more" stable than the tall one: it has a wider base and a lower centre of gravity, so S must be lifted further and tilted through a larger angle before it passes the edge (the book: the larger the base and the lower the centre of gravity, the more stable). The F_R = \mu\cdot F_N under it most likely notes that if you push such a low box sideways it slides (friction limits the push) before it tips; a tall box tips first. The box on its corner is in equilibrium, F_G and F_N on one vertical line, but the slightest tilt moves S past the contact point.

Unclear (p. 6): "locally stable"

The board labels the box balanced on its corner "locally stable", in quotation marks. In the book's terms this is unstable equilibrium, like the pencil on its tip: any small displacement lowers S and makes the box fall. The quotation marks suggest "it can stand there only at this one exact position". For the exam, use stable / unstable / neutral as defined above.

Worked example — how far can a cabinet tilt?

A cabinet is 1.8\ \mathrm m high and 0.60\ \mathrm m deep, uniform, so its centre of gravity S is in the middle: 0.90\ \mathrm m high, 0.30\ \mathrm m from the front edge.

  1. Critical position: it falls once S is vertically above the front edge, i.e. the line from the edge to S is vertical.
  2. Angle: in the upright cabinet that line makes the angle \varphi with the vertical where \tan\varphi = \frac{0.30}{0.90}, so \varphi = 18.4°. Tilted further than that, it tips over.
  3. Lying on its back (height 0.60\ \mathrm m, S at 0.30\ \mathrm m, 0.90\ \mathrm m from the edge): \tan\varphi = \frac{0.90}{0.30}, \varphi = 71.6°: far more stable.
Problem-solving steps — will it tip?
  1. Find the centre of gravity S (3 Center of Mass) and the edges of the base of support.
  2. Draw the vertical line through S: inside the base ⇒ stable (the weight's torque about the tipping edge turns it back); outside ⇒ it tips.
  3. Critical tilt angle: S directly above the edge, \tan\varphi = \dfrac{\text{horizontal distance S to edge}}{\text{height of S}}.
  4. If pushed sideways: compare the push needed to slide (\mu F_N) with the push needed to tip (torque about the edge) to see which happens first.

7 Continuum mechanics: solids, liquids, gases

Lecture: p. 6 middle · no matching Giancoli section (Giancoli Ch. 12–13, 17–18)

Until now every body was a point mass or a rigid body. The board's new heading, "CONTINUOUS MECHANICS" corrected to "continuum mechanics", treats matter as a continuous medium that can deform and flow. It splits by state of matter:

StateBranch (board)What it describes
Solid(solid) continuum mechanicsdeformation of solids: stress, strain, elasticity (sections 8–11)
Liquidfluid mechanicsflow, pressure
Gasthermodynamicstemperature, pressure, heat

The board adds "K = -273.15\,^\circ\mathrm C" and a sketch of a pipe that narrows and widens again, with arrows and "VELOCITY" marked at the narrow part.

Unclear (p. 6): "K = -273.15\,^\circ\mathrm C"

Taken literally, the line equates the unit kelvin with a temperature. What is meant is absolute zero: 0\ \mathrm K = -273.15\,^\circ\mathrm C, the lowest possible temperature, where the particles of the gas picture would stop moving (1 Physical Quantities and the SI System › 7 Accepted non-SI units and converting units: T/\mathrm K = \vartheta/{}^\circ\mathrm C + 273.15).

Intuition — the pipe sketch

A liquid can hardly be compressed, so the same volume per second must pass every cross-section of the pipe. Where the pipe is narrower, the liquid must flow faster: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 (the continuity equation of fluid mechanics, Giancoli Ch. 13). That is the "VELOCITY" mark at the constriction; it previews the fluid-mechanics part of the course.

8 The tensile test and the force–elongation curve

Lecture: p. 6 bottom – p. 7 top, p. 9 top · Giancoli §12-5

"SOLIDS → DEFORMABLE SOLIDS": every solid changes shape under a force. How much is measured in a tensile test: board sketch: a round specimen with thick ends for the grips and a thinner middle part of length L and diameter D; the machine pulls the ends apart with F (two red marks show the gauge length growing). The machine records the force F against the elongation \Delta L.

For small forces the elongation is proportional to the force, F = k\,\Delta L, like a spring (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 6 Work done by a varying force: the spring; for solids this is Hooke's law). In order along the curve:

  • elastic region: remove the force and the specimen returns to its original length;
  • proportional limit: up to here F \propto \Delta L exactly;
  • elastic limit / yield strength: beyond it the deformation is plastic, it stays after unloading (a bent paper clip);
  • ultimate strength: the maximum force the specimen carries;
  • breaking point: fracture.

Board sketches (p. 6–7): F–\Delta L curves for high-strength steel (rises steeply, high, breaks after little elongation) and ductile construction-grade steel (lower, with a wavy step, then a long plastic stretch before breaking ×); the step is circled in red and labelled "YIELD STRENGTH". Next to them the same curves as \sigma–\varepsilon.

Intuition — the wavy step of construction steel

Mild (construction) steel shows a distinct yield point: at a certain force the specimen suddenly stretches a little without needing more force (the zig-zag), before it hardens and needs more force again. High-strength steel has no such step: it is stronger but less ductile (less elongation before fracture). Ductility matters in buildings: a ductile beam bends visibly before it breaks; a brittle one breaks without warning.

9 Stress and strain

Lecture: p. 7 · Giancoli §12-5

The F–\Delta L curve depends on the specimen's size: a thicker bar needs more force, a longer bar stretches more. Dividing out the dimensions gives a curve of the material.

Stress — force per area, taken on the initial cross section (red on the board):

\sigma = \frac FA = \frac{F}{\frac{d_0^2\,\pi}{4}}, \qquad [\sigma] = \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm{mm^2}} \to \mathrm{Pa}, \qquad 1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m^2}, \qquad 1\ \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm{mm^2}} = 10^6\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{MPa}
Symbols
  • \sigma — (tensile) stress (N/mm² = MPa); the lecture's \sigma is the "engineering" stress, always referred to A = A_0
  • F — tensile force (N)
  • A = A_0 — initial cross-sectional area of the specimen (mm²); for a round bar A_0 = \frac{d_0^2\pi}4
  • d_0 — initial diameter (mm); the board's sketch writes D
  • Pa — pascal; 10^6\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{MPa} because 1\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}

Strain — the relative elongation:

\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0} = \frac{L(F) - L_0}{L_0}, \qquad \text{unitless},\quad [\varepsilon] = \%
Symbols
  • \varepsilon — strain, relative elongation (dimensionless, often given in %)
  • L_0 — initial (gauge) length (mm); L(F) — length under the force F (mm); \Delta L — elongation (mm)
Why divide by A_0 and L_0?

Two bars of the same steel, one with twice the cross-section: each half of the thick bar is a thin bar, so it needs twice the force for the same stretch. Force per area is the same. Two bars of different length under the same force: every centimetre stretches by the same amount, so the long bar stretches more in total, but the same fraction. So \sigma and \varepsilon don't depend on the specimen's size, and the \sigma–\varepsilon curve belongs to the material: one test, valid for every part made of it.

The stress–strain curve. Board diagram, \sigma(F) against \varepsilon/\Delta L: a straight first part ("LINEAR", "linear elastic behaviour"); its end marked "yield strength"; the curve then bends over to a maximum, "UTS: ultimate tensile strength", and ends shortly after at fracture (×, circled red). On the strain axis: "0.2%" below the start, a red line parallel to the straight part starting there, "10–15%" spanning to the region of the maximum, and the regions "elastic deformation" (left) and "plastic deformation" (right).

Filling the gaps — the red lines and the "0.2 %"

Unloading: if the specimen is loaded beyond the yield strength and then unloaded, it does not go back along the curve: it comes down along a line parallel to the elastic straight line (the red line from the red dot on the board) and ends at a strain > 0. That remaining strain is the plastic (permanent) deformation; only the elastic part springs back. 0.2 % yield strength: many metals have no sharp yield point, so the yield strength is defined by convention: draw a line parallel to the elastic part, starting at \varepsilon = 0.2\,\%; where it cuts the curve is the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.2 % after unloading (R_{p0.2} in German standards). That is the board's "0.2 %" with the parallel line. 10–15 %: the order of magnitude of the strain at the maximum / at fracture for a ductile steel; compare with the elastic strains, far below 1 %.

Unclear (p. 7): "10–15 %" and "usually … 2 %"

The arrow "← 10–15 % →" is not clearly anchored on the axis; read above as the strain reached near the maximum or at fracture of a ductile steel. Below, under "USUALLY", a second sketch shows a curve rising steeply to the yield strength "YS", with UTS slightly higher, and "2 %" marked on the strain axis under the UTS. Most likely it says that for many (high-strength) materials yield and ultimate strength are close and the curve ends after only a few per cent of strain; the exact meaning of "2 %" was not written down.

10 Young's modulus and Hooke's law

Lecture: p. 7 bottom – p. 8 · Giancoli §12-5

Board sketch: several straight lines from the origin in a \sigma–\varepsilon diagram with different slopes; at one of them a slope triangle marked E; one line continued (dotted) up to "100 %"; "k\uparrow … stiffness goes up". The slope of the elastic straight line is Young's modulus ("E … Y … Young's modulus": Giancoli writes E, some books Y). A steeper line means a stiffer material: more stress for the same strain.

[Y], [E] = \mathrm{MPa},\ \mathrm{Pa},\ \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm{mm^2}}, \qquad E_\text{steel} = 210\,000\ \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm{mm^2}}\ \text{or MPa}
Symbols
  • E (or Y) — Young's modulus (elastic modulus) of the material (N/mm² = MPa, or Pa); 1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{N/m^2}
  • E_\text{steel} = 210\,000\ \mathrm{MPa} = 210\ \mathrm{GPa} = 2.1\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}; Giancoli's table gives 200\cdot10^9\ \mathrm{N/m^2} for steel (alloys differ slightly)

Board, under E_\text{steel}: "elastic stress to achieve 100 % of \varepsilon".

Filling the gaps — what "100 % of \varepsilon" means

Since E is a slope, E = \sigma/\varepsilon, it equals the stress at \varepsilon = 1 = 100\,\% if the straight line were continued (the dotted line to "100 %" on the board): the stress that would double the bar's length. It's a thought experiment only: real steel yields at a few hundred N/mm², at a strain of about 0.1–0.2\,\%, and never gets anywhere near 100 % elastically. The definition just makes the unit of E plausible: a strain is unitless, so E has the unit of a stress.

The straight line is Hooke's law for materials (boxed on the board), in the same form as y = k\cdot x for a straight line through the origin, and as F = k x for a spring:

\boxed{\ \sigma = E\,\varepsilon\ } \qquad (y = E\cdot x,\quad y = k\cdot x)
Symbols
  • \sigma — stress (N/mm²), the "y" of the diagram; \varepsilon — strain (dimensionless), the "x"
  • E — Young's modulus (N/mm²), the slope "k"; valid only in the linear elastic range

Inserting the definitions \sigma = \frac F{A_0} and \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0} (boxed, with an arrow to \Delta L, the quantity usually asked for):

\boxed{\ \frac{F}{A_0} = E\cdot\frac{\Delta L}{L_0}\ } \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \Delta L = \frac{F\cdot L_0}{E\cdot A_0}
Symbols
  • F — tensile force (N); A_0 — initial cross-section (mm²); L_0 — initial length (mm); \Delta L — elongation (mm)
  • E — Young's modulus (N/mm²); the right-hand form is solved for \Delta L (multiply by L_0/E)
Intuition — a bar is a spring

Compare with F = k\,\Delta L: a bar is a spring with stiffness k = \frac{E A_0}{L_0}. Thicker bar (larger A_0): stiffer. Longer bar (larger L_0): softer. Stiffer material (larger E): stiffer. Every factor of that formula is something you can feel when you pull on a wire.

Worked example — how much does a steel tie rod stretch?

A round steel rod, d_0 = 10\ \mathrm{mm}, L_0 = 2.0\ \mathrm m, carries F = 10\ \mathrm{kN}.

  1. Cross-section: A_0 = \frac{d_0^2\pi}4 = \frac{10^2\cdot\pi}{4} = 78.5\ \mathrm{mm^2}.
  2. Stress: \sigma = \frac F{A_0} = \frac{10\,000\ \mathrm N}{78.5\ \mathrm{mm^2}} = 127\ \mathrm{N/mm^2} = 127\ \mathrm{MPa}: well below the strength of steel, so the linear elastic law applies.
  3. Strain: \varepsilon = \frac\sigma E = \frac{127}{210\,000} = 6.1\cdot10^{-4} = 0.061\,\%.
  4. Elongation: \Delta L = \varepsilon L_0 = 6.1\cdot10^{-4}\cdot2000\ \mathrm{mm} = 1.2\ \mathrm{mm}. Units: N/mm² throughout, so no conversions are needed (work in N and mm).
Common mistake — stiffness and strength are the same thing

Young's modulus E says how much a material stretches under load (stiffness); the yield and ultimate strength say how much load it survives (strength). High-strength and construction steel have almost the same E (same slope at the start of the board's curves) but very different strengths. And stress, strain and E are different things: pulling harder raises \sigma and \varepsilon, while E, a property of the material, stays the same.

Problem-solving steps — tension in a bar
  1. Compute A_0 from the initial dimensions (round: \frac{d_0^2\pi}4).
  2. Stress \sigma = F/A_0; work in N and mm to get N/mm² = MPa directly.
  3. Check that \sigma is below the yield strength (otherwise \sigma = E\varepsilon doesn't hold), and, with a safety factor, below the ultimate strength.
  4. Strain \varepsilon = \sigma/E, elongation \Delta L = \varepsilon L_0 (or \Delta L = \frac{F L_0}{E A_0} in one step).

11 Strength of materials

Lecture: p. 9 bottom · Giancoli §12-6

The lecture closes with the textbook's table of ultimate strengths (maximum stress before fracture) under tension, compression and shear (pasted, p. 9):

MaterialTensile strength (N/m²)Compressive strength (N/m²)Shear strength (N/m²)
Iron, cast170\cdot10^6550\cdot10^6170\cdot10^6
Steel500\cdot10^6500\cdot10^6250\cdot10^6
Brass250\cdot10^6250\cdot10^6200\cdot10^6
Aluminum200\cdot10^6200\cdot10^6200\cdot10^6
Concrete2\cdot10^620\cdot10^62\cdot10^6
Brick35\cdot10^6

Wood (pine), parallel to grain40\cdot10^635\cdot10^65\cdot10^6

(Giancoli Table 12-2.) In the lecture's units, 10^6\ \mathrm{N/m^2} = 1\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}: steel breaks at about 500\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}, concrete in tension at only 2\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}.

Intuition — reading the table

Concrete and stone are ten times stronger in compression than in tension: they make good columns and arches but bad beams (the lower side of a sagging beam is stretched). That is why concrete beams get steel bars where the tension is. And the values are typical, not guaranteed: engineers design with a safety factor of about 3–10, i.e. the working stress stays at a third to a tenth of the table value.

Worked example — when would the tie rod break?

The rod of section 10 (A_0 = 78.5\ \mathrm{mm^2}) made of typical steel, ultimate tensile strength 500\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}:

  1. Breaking force: F_\text{max} = 500\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}\cdot78.5\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 39\,000\ \mathrm N = 39\ \mathrm{kN}.
  2. Safety factor at 10 kN: 39/10 \approx 3.9, within the usual 3–10.
